summary:
ASTRAIL is an interactive Martian mapping and mission-planning application designed to support crewed and robotic expeditions across complex terrains like Eos Chaos.

Using an interactive map, mission planners and astronauts can set start and end coordinates, inspect elevation profiles, and evaluate route risk levels (low, medium, or high) to receive automated path recommendations. Additionally, an integrated mission report module tracks scientific research objectives, logs progress, and compiles expedition results in real time.

This tool is vital for the future of Mars exploration. By combining terrain risk analysis with scientific task management in a single intuitive interface, ASTRAIL minimizes hazards to rovers and crews, optimizes travel time, and ensures that critical research goals are achieved safely and efficiently.
details:
1. What does it do or how does it work? ASTRAIL is an interplanetary navigation and scientific exploration concept prototype designed to help astronauts plan safer routes on Mars. It bridges global planetary data with local field planning through three core modules: Main screen (displays mission goals, environmental conditions, hazards, and interactive maps), Route Analysis (compares terrain risks, elevation profiles, and route metrics), and Mission report (manages research points and scientific tasks). The workflow consists of three simple steps:

  1. Select a Mission: The astronaut or mission planner chooses a specific scientific objective and research location (such as an expedition to Eos Chaos).
  2. Generate Routes: The system generates and displays three alternative route options to the destination with different risk profiles (low, medium, and high risk).
  3. Compare & Select: The user compares distance, estimated travel time, elevation profiles, and terrain hazards to make an informed, safe decision. (Note: The current prototype uses real Mars surface imagery combined with illustrative, conceptual route simulations.)

2. What benefits does it have?

  • Unified Data Access: Consolidates scattered scientific and terrain information from different NASA missions into one clear, intuitive dashboard.
  • Enhanced Crew Safety: Highlights hazardous terrain—such as steep slopes, sharp rocks, strong winds, sand traps, and unstable ground—before astronauts enter the field.
  • Informed Decision-Making: Gives crews three distinct route options instead of a single path, allowing them to balance travel speed against safety and scientific value.
  • External use: The ability to use the application outdoors via Spacesuit mode.

3. What is the intended impact of the project? The primary goal of ASTRAIL is to make future human exploration of Mars safer, smarter, and more scientifically productive. By translating complex orbital and geological Mars data into easy-to-understand visual guidance, the system reduces cognitive load on astronauts and minimizes navigation risks. Ultimately, it directly connects safe route planning with scientific objectives, enabling crews to reach high-value research targets efficiently. In future development stages, the concept can scale to integrate live, verified NASA telemetry and automated terrain-based pathfinding algorithms.

4. What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use to develop your project?

  • Design & Prototyping Software: Figma — used for full UI/UX design, interactive prototyping, and creating the project presentation.
  • AI Assistance: ChatGPT and Gemini — utilized for brainstorming concepts, structuring ideas, and refining project texts.
  • Data & Reference Sources: Real Mars surface imagery sourced from NASA Mars Trek and official NASA Space Apps Challenge resources.

5. How is your project creative? ASTRAIL stands out by combining scientific mission management with human-centered interface design specifically tailored for planetary exploration. Instead of overwhelming astronauts with raw, fragmented datasets, we reimagined navigation as a clear visual comparison of three risk-tiered routes paired with mission-specific scientific tasks. Creative UI details—like topographic background motifs, color-coded hazard indicators, elevation charts, and a dedicated "Spacesuit mode" button for quick accessibility—demonstrate practical empathy for end-users operating in harsh extraterrestrial environments.

6. What factors did your team consider?

  • Terrain: actual distances and elevations calculated via Mars Trek
  • Environmental & Terrain Hazards: Steep slopes, sharp rock fragments, soft/unstable ground, sand traps, and strong Martian winds.
  • Data Fragmentation: The challenge of uniting dispersed scientific data from multiple NASA tools into a single, actionable field interface.
  • Human Factors: High-stress decision-making during missions.
  • Scientific Value vs. Safety: A combination of goals, time savings, and safety.
  • Technical Transparency: Clearly distinguishing between real NASA reference imagery and conceptual prototype simulations while outlining a realistic roadmap for future data integration.
